name: Civil / Non-religious
blurb: A wedding shaped entirely by you: a registrar or celebrant, your own vows, readings and music, and no religious framework unless you choose to borrow from one.

events.name: Engagement party
events.when: Within a few months of the engagement
events.description: An informal gathering to celebrate the engagement, at home, in a pub or restaurant, or as a bigger party. There is no set form; some couples use it as the moment the two families and friendship groups first mix.

events.name: Hen and stag celebrations
events.description: Called a bachelorette and bachelor party in the US and a hen and stag do in Britain and Ireland. Increasingly mixed or joint, and anything from one night out to a weekend away. Usually organised and paid for by the wedding party rather than the couple.

events.name: Venue walkthrough or rehearsal
events.when: A day or two before, or the week of the wedding
events.description: Civil weddings rarely have a formal rehearsal; the registrars brief you on the day and interview each of you privately before the ceremony. Celebrant-led couples more often do a short run-through, since the celebrant controls the running order. Even without one, a walkthrough of the space with your coordinator settles nerves and timings.

events.name: Statutory marriage at the register office
events.when: Days or weeks before, or the same morning
events.description: The legal two-step for celebrant-led couples in England and Wales: a short, basic register office ceremony with just the two of you and two witnesses, which makes you legally married, followed by the celebrant ceremony everyone will remember. Councils run these on limited days, with no music or readings and no extra guests. You can do it before, after or on the morning of the main ceremony; most couples do it a few days before.

events.name: First look
events.description: A private, photographed moment where you see each other before the ceremony instead of at the top of the aisle. It calms nerves, and it lets couple portraits happen before guests arrive, freeing up the drinks reception. Entirely a matter of taste; plenty of couples still prefer the aisle reveal.

events.name: The ceremony
events.description: Typically 20 to 45 minutes. A registrar-led civil ceremony includes the required legal declarations plus any non-religious readings, music and personal vows you have agreed in advance; two witnesses must be present and you sign the marriage schedule. A celebrant-led ceremony is written from scratch around your story and can include anything you like, anywhere you like, but in England and Wales it is not itself legally binding.

events.name: Drinks reception
events.description: An hour or two of drinks and canapés while photographs happen and the room is turned around for the meal. At a single-venue wedding this is the natural congratulations moment, since there is no journey between ceremony and reception.

events.name: Wedding breakfast and speeches
events.description: The main meal, still called the wedding breakfast in Britain whatever the hour. Speeches traditionally run father of the bride, then the groom, then the best man, but civil weddings freely reorder this: couples speak together, mothers and maids of honour speak, or speeches move to between courses.
events.hosts: Traditionally the couple or their parents; now usually the couple

events.name: Evening reception
events.description: The cake cutting, first dance, band or DJ, and evening food. Many British couples invite a second, larger guest list for the evening only, which lets colleagues and the wider circle join without a bigger seated meal.

events.name: Day-after gathering
events.description: A relaxed brunch, pub lunch or barbecue for close family and guests who travelled. Common when the venue has accommodation or the wedding is a weekend away; not expected otherwise.

items.name: Notice of marriage fees
items.note: The statutory fee each of you pays to give notice at the register office. In England and Wales it is charged per person and is higher if either of you is referred for immigration checks. Scotland, Northern Ireland and Ireland have their own equivalent notice or notification fees. Small, but easy to forget.

items.name: Registrar and ceremony fee
items.note: What the registration service charges for the ceremony itself. A register office ceremony room is the cheapest route; registrars attending an approved venue cost noticeably more, and most councils price weekends above weekdays. This is booked with and paid to the council, separately from anything the venue charges.

items.name: Celebrant fee
items.note: For a celebrant-led ceremony: the fee covers meetings, writing a script from scratch around you, editing it with you, the day itself and often a rehearsal. Humanist celebrants (through Humanists UK or Humanist Society Scotland) keep the ceremony entirely non-religious; independent celebrants will blend in religious or spiritual elements if you want them. In Scotland and Northern Ireland an authorised humanist celebrant can also legally marry you, so there is no separate registrar ceremony to pay for.

items.name: Statutory ceremony fee
items.note: The basic register office ceremony that makes a celebrant-led wedding legally binding in England and Wales. It usually includes the registrars and one marriage certificate. Only needed if your main ceremony is celebrant-led; skip it if a registrar is conducting your wedding, or if you are marrying in Scotland or Northern Ireland with an authorised celebrant.

items.name: Marriage certificate copies
items.note: In England and Wales certificates are no longer handed over on the day: the signed schedule goes back to the register office, the marriage is registered electronically and certificates are posted afterwards. Order two or three copies, because banks, passport offices and employers often want to see an original when you change your name.

items.name: Ceremony room or space hire
items.note: Many venues charge separately for the ceremony room or outdoor ceremony area on top of the main venue hire, and register offices charge more for their larger, prettier rooms than for the basic one. If your ceremony and reception are in different places, cost both.

items.name: Ceremony musicians
items.note: A string quartet, acoustic guitarist, pianist or singer for the entrance, signing and exit. Entirely optional: recorded music through the venue's system is normal and most registration services simply ask for your choices in advance. In England and Wales the pieces played at a registrar-led ceremony must not be religious.

items.name: Symbolic ceremony supplies
items.note: The kit for any symbolic act you add: handfasting cords or ribbons, a sand-blending set, a memory or wine box, a quaich, or a tree and soil. All optional, and cheap compared with almost everything else on this list. If a registrar is conducting the ceremony, clear the addition with the registration service first.

items.name: Destination wedding legal documents
items.note: If you marry abroad: a certificate of no impediment where the country asks for one, apostille legalisation, certified translations, and courier fees. Requirements differ sharply by country, and some have their own residency periods. Many couples avoid the whole stack by marrying legally at home and holding the celebration abroad.

items.name: Venue hire
items.note: For civil weddings the ceremony and reception are very often under one roof, which is the main structural difference from a church wedding: one venue, no travel, and in England and Wales the venue must be on the council's approved premises list if you are marrying there. Exclusive-use country houses and barns charge most; hotels often offset hire against catering minimums; dry-hire spaces look cheap until you add everything they do not include.

items.name: Wedding meal
items.note: Usually the single largest line. Check what the per-head price actually includes: staffing, linen, cake cutting, corkage and service charge are the usual quiet extras. Dietary requirements are simpler to handle at a civil wedding than couples fear; caterers deal with them daily.

items.name: Drinks and bar
items.note: Reception drinks, wine with the meal, a toast drink and whatever you put behind the bar. Note one rule that surprises people at approved premises in England and Wales: alcohol cannot be sold or consumed in the ceremony area immediately before or during the ceremony, so the welcome drinks wait until you are married.

items.name: Evening food
items.note: The late spread for dancers and evening guests: bacon rolls, pizza, a cheese table, a food truck. If you invite a separate evening guest list, budget this per evening head, not per daytime head.

items.name: Wedding cake
items.note: Cut together as one of the evening's marker moments, often photographed just before the first dance. Some couples replace it with a cheese tower, doughnut wall or dessert table; nothing about a civil wedding requires a cake at all.

items.name: Day-after gathering
items.note: Brunch, a pub lunch or a barbecue for those staying over. Keep it informal and self-serve; after a wedding, nobody wants a second seating plan.

items.name: Wedding dress or first outfit
items.note: No dress code comes with a civil wedding: full gown, jumpsuit, suit or something entirely your own all work. Made-to-order dresses need six months or more plus alterations; off-the-peg and second-hand are increasingly normal and free up budget elsewhere.

items.name: Partner's outfit
items.note: Bought or hired suit, tuxedo or a second dress. Hiring makes sense if the wedding party is matching; buying makes sense if you will wear it again.

items.name: Shoes, veil and accessories
items.note: Shoes, jewellery, and a veil if you want one; plenty of civil brides skip the veil entirely. If your ceremony is outdoors on grass, think about heels before the day does it for you.

items.name: Wedding party outfits
items.note: Bridesmaids, groomsmen, flower girls and page boys, if you have them; a civil wedding can just as easily have no wedding party at all. Who pays varies by family. Mismatched-but-coordinating outfits have made this line cheaper for many couples.

items.name: Hair and make-up
items.note: A trial beforehand plus the wedding morning. Book the trial around the time of your final dress fitting so the whole look comes together at once.

items.name: Wedding party hair and make-up
items.note: Priced per head for bridesmaids and mothers. Decide early whether you are treating or they are paying, and confirm numbers before the stylist books a second artist.

items.name: Bouquets and buttonholes
items.note: Bouquet, bridesmaids' flowers, buttonholes and corsages for parents. Dried and silk flowers are common at civil weddings and survive the day rather better than they used to.

items.name: Ceremony flowers and arch
items.note: An arch, arrangement or aisle flowers to frame the ceremony spot, which matters more at a civil wedding because the backdrop is whatever you make it rather than a church. Choose pieces that can move: most florists will relocate the arch flowers to the top table or cake area during the drinks reception.

items.name: Reception flowers and styling
items.note: Centrepieces, top table flowers and general styling. Because a civil wedding usually happens in one venue, one coherent look carries the whole day, which is simpler and often cheaper than dressing two locations.

items.name: Lighting and dance floor
items.note: Festoon lights, uplighting or a hired dance floor. Most relevant for marquees, barns and dry-hire spaces; hotels usually come dressed.

items.name: Signage and decor extras
items.note: Welcome sign, seating chart display, table names, candles and the odd neon sign. Small individually; keep a single decor list or this category multiplies quietly.

items.name: Photographer
items.note: Civil ceremonies are generally relaxed about photography, but the registrars or celebrant run the room, so have your photographer introduce themselves before the ceremony and agree where they can stand. If you are doing a first look or a two-step wedding, make sure the coverage hours match the real shape of your day.

items.name: Videographer
items.note: Highlights film or full-ceremony edit. Personal vows are the thing couples most often wish they had on film, so if the budget only stretches to partial coverage, cover the ceremony and speeches.

items.name: Photo booth
items.note: A booth or backdrop with props for the evening. Doubles as a guest book if the booth prints two copies, one for guests and one for an album they sign.

items.name: Band or main entertainment
items.note: A live band for the evening is the classic centrepiece, but civil weddings go every direction: DJ only, a ceilidh caller, an acoustic act that plays daytime and evening. Check the venue's sound limiter and licensed finish time before you book anything loud or late.

items.name: DJ
items.note: Either the main event or the act that takes over between and after band sets. A good DJ takes requests and reads the room; send a short do-not-play list rather than a full playlist.

items.name: Daytime entertainment
items.note: Lawn games, a magician, a caricaturist or live music for the drinks reception. Most useful when portraits will take you away from guests for a stretch.

items.name: Invitations and save the dates
items.note: Printed, digital or a mix; many couples now run RSVPs through a free wedding website and print only the main invitation. If you have separate daytime and evening guest lists, you need two versions, and the difference should be unmissable.

items.name: On-the-day stationery
items.note: Order of the day, place cards, menus and the table plan. A civil order of service is short, one card rather than a booklet, and entirely optional.

items.name: Wedding cars
items.note: Transport to the ceremony, and between venues if you have two. At a single-venue wedding many couples skip cars entirely or hire one for the arrival photographs only.

items.name: Guest transport
items.note: A coach or minibus at the end of the night is money well spent when the venue is rural, and some venues in remote spots effectively require it. Less necessary at town-centre venues near taxis and hotels.

items.name: Wedding rings
items.note: Exchanged during the ceremony by long custom, though no law in the UK requires rings at all: the marriage is made by the declarations and the signatures. One ring, two rings or none are all fine, and your celebrant or registrar will shape the wording to match.

items.name: Gifts for the wedding party and parents
items.note: Thank-yous for attendants, parents, readers and your witnesses. Witnesses are worth remembering here: at a civil wedding they have a genuine legal role, and a small gift acknowledges it.

items.name: Favours
items.note: A small token at each place setting. Entirely optional and one of the first lines couples cut; a charity donation card per table is a common replacement.

items.name: Wedding insurance
items.note: Covers supplier failure, cancellation, illness and damage. Buy it when you pay your first deposit, not the month before the wedding, because cover starts from purchase. Some venues and marquee companies also require you to hold public liability cover.

items.name: Wedding night accommodation
items.note: Your room, and possibly rooms for parents or the wedding party. If the venue offers a bedroom block, find out who pays if guests do not fill it; that clause catches people out.

items.name: Planner or on-the-day coordinator
items.note: A full planner suits complicated or long-distance weddings; an on-the-day coordinator suits couples who have planned everything and want to hand over the running of it. Dry-hire venues without in-house staff are where a coordinator earns their fee most obviously.

items.name: Confetti
items.note: The confetti exit is one of the defining photographs of a civil wedding. Most venues insist on dried petals or other biodegradable confetti and ban the paper kind, so check the rule and tell guests, or supply it yourself in cones.

timeline.task: Decide the shape of the day: register office, an approved venue with a registrar, or a celebrant-led ceremony with a separate statutory marriage (England and Wales) or a legally authorised celebrant (Scotland and Northern Ireland)
Agree the overall budget and rough guest numbers with everyone contributing
In England and Wales, check the registration service's availability for your date before you confirm the venue: the registrar and the venue are separate bookings and both must line up
Book the venue, checking it is on the council's approved premises list if a registrar is marrying you there in England or Wales
Book the registrars' attendance with the council, or book your celebrant
Take out wedding insurance as soon as the first deposits are paid
Book the photographer and videographer
Book the band or DJ, checking the venue's sound limiter and finish time first
Start outfit shopping; made-to-order dresses need six months or more plus alterations
Send save the dates, especially if guests are travelling
Book the florist, and the caterer if your venue is dry hire
If marrying abroad, research that country's legal requirements, residency rules and paperwork now, and decide whether to do the legal marriage at home instead
Start shaping the ceremony: choose readings, music and any symbolic elements, and begin the script with your celebrant if you have one
In England and Wales, send your proposed music and readings to the registration service for approval, since religious content is not allowed and decisions vary between districts
Order invitations
Send invitations, making the daytime and evening guest distinction unmissable if you have one

Give notice: in England and Wales at your local register office at least 29 days before the ceremony (valid 12 months); in Scotland submit M10 forms no later than 29 days and no earlier than 3 months before; in Northern Ireland at least 28 days before
Buy the wedding rings, or decide you are not having them
Hair and make-up trial, timed near a dress fitting
Choose your two witnesses and tell them what the role involves
Write your personal vows and share them with your celebrant, or check what additions your registrar allows
Confirm final numbers with the caterer and the running order with the venue
Final venue meeting: confirm registrar or celebrant arrival time, the pre-ceremony interview, and where the signing table goes
If your main ceremony is celebrant-led in England or Wales, confirm the statutory register office booking and the witnesses attending it
In Scotland, collect the marriage schedule in person from the register office in the seven days before the wedding; in Northern Ireland collect it no more than 14 days before
Walk through the ceremony space, or hold a short rehearsal if your celebrant offers one

paperwork.note: Given in person at a register office in the district where you live, after living there for at least the past 7 days. It must be given at least 29 days before the ceremony, the notice is publicly displayed at the register office, and the ceremony must happen within 12 months. If you live in different districts you each give notice in your own.

A valid passport or UK birth certificate, plus proof of address such as a driving licence, utility bill, bank statement or tenancy agreement. If you were born after 1 January 1983 and use a UK birth certificate, you may also need evidence of a parent's nationality.

paperwork.item: Evidence a previous marriage or civil partnership has ended
paperwork.note: A decree absolute or final order, or the former partner's death certificate. Divorces granted outside the UK have to be checked by the registration service, which carries a fee and can add time, so raise it at the start rather than at the notice appointment.
A deed poll or equivalent, so the names on your documents line up.

paperwork.who: Any partner who is not a British or Irish citizen without settled or pre-settled status
paperwork.note: You must give notice together at a designated register office, bring passport photos and evidence of immigration status, and translations of any documents not in English. The standard waiting period can be extended from 29 to 70 days if the Home Office decides to investigate, so build slack into the timeline.

Since May 2021 you sign a marriage schedule at the ceremony rather than a register book. The registrar takes it away, the marriage is entered in an electronic register, and up to four parents' names (mothers included) can appear on the record.
No longer handed over on the day in England and Wales; they are posted after the marriage is registered. Order extra certified copies for passports, banks and name changes.

Each of you submits an M10 to the registrar for the district where the ceremony will be held, no later than 29 days and no earlier than 3 months before. There is no residency requirement in Scotland; couples from anywhere may marry there.

One of you must collect it in person from the register office in the seven days before the wedding; nobody can collect it for you. It is signed after the ceremony by you both, the celebrant and two witnesses aged 16 or over, and must be returned to the register office within three days.

Submitted to the registrar for the district where the ceremony takes place, at least 28 days before and no more than a year ahead; registration offices recommend around 12 to 14 weeks. The schedule is collected in person no more than 14 days before the ceremony and returned within three working days after it.

You must notify a civil registrar (HSE) at least three months before the wedding, usually in person, and you receive a Marriage Registration Form that the solemniser needs on the day. Humanist Association of Ireland celebrants have been legal solemnisers since 2012.

paperwork.item: Statutory ceremony booking (England and Wales two-step)
paperwork.who: Both, if your main ceremony is celebrant-led
paperwork.note: The short register office ceremony that makes the marriage legal. Councils run them on limited days with only your two witnesses attending, so book it when you book the celebrant, not as an afterthought.

paperwork.who: Both, if marrying abroad and the country requires one
paperwork.note: Issued after you give notice at your local register office; only British nationals can get one this way, and other nationals should ask their embassy. Check with the country's authorities how long it stays valid, as this varies.

paperwork.item: Legalisation and translations for marrying abroad
paperwork.note: Many countries require your documents to be legalised with an apostille and translated by a certified translator. Allow weeks rather than days, and check whether the translations themselves need legalising.

A marriage legally performed abroad is recognised in the UK provided it followed local law and you were both free to marry; there is no requirement, and no facility, to register it in the UK afterwards. Keep the original certificate and a certified translation safe, and buy spare certified copies before you leave the country.

customs.name: Personal vows
customs.description: Promises you write yourselves, spoken alongside the required legal declarations rather than instead of them. Registrars allow non-religious additions to the set wording; celebrants build the whole ceremony around them. Keep a printed copy each; almost nobody trusts memory on the day.

customs.name: The celebrant tells your story
customs.description: The heart of most celebrant-led and humanist ceremonies: the celebrant recounts how you met and who you are as a couple, gathered from meetings and questionnaires beforehand. It is the part guests most often say they remember.

customs.name: First look
customs.description: Seeing each other privately before the ceremony, usually photographed. A deliberate modern swap for the aisle reveal, chosen for calm nerves and better use of the day; couples who prefer the traditional moment simply skip it.

customs.name: Walking in together
customs.description: Many couples now enter side by side, or each walk in with a parent, or with both parents, rather than one waiting at the front. There is no rule; a civil ceremony lets you stage the entrance any way that feels honest.

customs.name: Handfasting
customs.description: The couple's hands are loosely bound with cords or ribbons while promises are made, a practice with Celtic roots and the likely origin of 'tying the knot'. Used in entirely secular form at many humanist and celebrant ceremonies, sometimes with family members each laying a ribbon.

customs.name: Sand blending
customs.description: Each of you pours coloured sand into one vessel, the layers standing for two lives combined; children from either side are often given their own colour so the whole new family pours together. A modern, secular unity ritual.

customs.name: Unity candle
customs.description: Two side candles used to light one central candle. It has church origins in some countries but is used in a fully secular form at civil and celebrant ceremonies; outdoor couples learn quickly that wind is its natural enemy.

customs.name: Ring warming
customs.description: The rings are passed among guests, or hung where guests can hold them, so everyone briefly holds them and wishes you well before the exchange. Works best at smaller ceremonies where the rings can genuinely travel the room and return in time.

customs.name: Wine box or letter ceremony
customs.description: You seal a bottle and letters to each other in a box during the ceremony, to be opened on a future anniversary. A celebrant-era invention with no religious content, and a favourite for couples who want a ritual object to keep.

customs.name: Tree planting
customs.description: You pot or plant a tree together, sometimes with soil from each family's home. Suits outdoor and garden weddings, and leaves you with something that grows; check the logistics of moving it afterwards.

customs.name: The quaich
customs.description: A two-handled Scottish cup shared as a first drink together, each holding one handle, as a sign of trust. Traditional at Scottish weddings and borrowed well beyond them.

customs.name: Readings by guests
customs.description: Friends and family read poems, prose or song lyrics during the ceremony. At a registrar-led ceremony in England and Wales the readings must be non-religious; celebrant ceremonies have no restrictions at all.

customs.name: Confetti exit
customs.description: Guests shower you with petals or paper shapes as you leave the ceremony or the venue. Most venues now require biodegradable confetti or dried petals, so supply it in cones and tell the photographer where the throw will happen.

customs.name: Receiving line
customs.description: The couple, and traditionally both sets of parents, greet every guest in turn before the meal. Falling out of fashion because it is slow at large weddings; many couples replace it by visiting tables during the meal.

customs.name: Speeches
customs.description: The traditional British order is father of the bride, groom, best man, ending with toasts. Civil weddings rearrange freely: both partners speak, a maid of honour speaks, parents share a toast, or speeches are dropped entirely. Tell speakers a time limit and mean it.

customs.name: First dance
customs.description: The couple open the dancing to a chosen song, often followed by parent dances in families that keep that custom. Couples who dread it choose a short song, invite everyone onto the floor after the first minute, or skip it without ceremony.

customs.name: Cutting the cake
customs.description: The couple make the first cut together, usually photographed, often just before the first dance so the evening moments run in sequence. The old custom of saving a tier has faded along with fruit cake, but nothing stops you.

customs.name: Unplugged ceremony
customs.description: Guests are asked to put phones and cameras away for the ceremony so the photographer's shots are clear of screens and everyone is actually watching. Announced by a sign, the celebrant or the registrar's introduction.

customs.name: Something old, something new
customs.description: The rhyme continues 'something borrowed, something blue', each item worn or carried for luck. A folk custom with no religious content, kept alive because it gives mothers, grandmothers and friends a way into the wedding morning.

customs.name: The night before apart
customs.description: Spending the last night in separate places and not seeing each other until the ceremony. Pure superstition and widely ignored by couples who would rather wake up together; the first look exists partly because this custom loosened.

customs.name: Gift lists and honeymoon funds
customs.description: Couples who already share a home increasingly ask for contributions to the honeymoon or a house fund instead of a traditional gift list, usually via a line on the invitation or wedding website. Cash in cards remains completely normal in many families.

gotchas: In England and Wales a celebrant-led or humanist ceremony is not legally binding on its own. You also need a legal marriage before a registrar, usually a short statutory ceremony at the register office. Budget for both and put both in the diary.

The UK Government announced in October 2025 that it intends to give humanist marriages legal recognition in England and Wales, but with further consultation planned the law has not yet changed. Plan on the two-step unless your registration service confirms otherwise.

In Scotland the position is different: Humanist Society Scotland and other authorised belief celebrants have legally married couples since 2005, and in Northern Ireland humanist marriages have been legal since 2018. No separate registrar ceremony is needed there.

The registrar and the venue are separate bookings in England and Wales. Couples book a venue, announce the date, and only then discover no registrar is free. Check ceremony availability with the registration service before you pay a venue deposit.

You give notice in the district where you live, not where you are marrying, and you must have lived there for the previous 7 days. Both of you attend in person. If you live in different districts you each give notice in your own.

Notice in England and Wales is valid for only 12 months, so with a long engagement you cannot give notice when you book; the venue may be booked two years out while the legal clock cannot start until the final year.

If either of you is not a British or Irish citizen and has no settled status, you must give notice together at a designated register office, and the waiting period can be extended from 29 to 70 days for Home Office checks. Do not book a date inside that window.

A civil ceremony in England and Wales must contain nothing religious: no hymns, no scripture, and registrars vet your music and readings in advance. Songs with a passing mention of heaven or angels are treated differently from district to district, so submit your choices early rather than argue on the day.

Outdoor ceremonies in England and Wales are legal only within the grounds of approved premises, in an outdoor area the venue has agreed with the registrar, who must consider it seemly and dignified. A beach, a park or your own back garden is not an option unless it is part of licensed premises, and private homes generally cannot be licensed. In Scotland, by contrast, you can marry anywhere you and the celebrant or registrar agree.

A statutory register office ceremony is deliberately minimal: limited days and times, only your two witnesses present, no music, no readings, no personalisation. Treat it as the legal step, not a small wedding, and save the meaning for your main ceremony.

In England and Wales you no longer get a marriage certificate on the day. The schedule is registered electronically and certificates are posted afterwards, so do not book anything that needs proof of marriage, like a passport in a new name, for the days straight after the wedding.

Witnesses must be able to see and understand what is happening, and most registration services ask that they be at least 16. Choose them in advance; pulling in a stranger works legally but makes for an odd photograph and an odder story.

At approved premises in England and Wales, alcohol cannot be sold or consumed in the ceremony area in the period immediately before and during the ceremony, so plan the welcome drinks for after the legal part, not before.

Marrying in Scotland has no residency requirement, which is why couples travel there, but the schedule must be collected in person by one of you in the seven days before the wedding and returned within three days after. For a destination-Scotland wedding that means arriving early enough to collect it.

For a destination wedding, the country's own rules govern everything: some require weeks of residence, most require legalised and translated documents, and a certificate of no impediment takes time because it follows the notice process at home. Many couples marry legally at home first and treat the ceremony abroad as a celebration, which removes the paperwork risk.

A marriage validly performed abroad is already recognised in the UK; you cannot register it here and you cannot legally marry the same person again in the UK to be safe. Buy several certified copies of the certificate and a certified translation before leaving the country, because getting them later from abroad is slow.

Humanist celebrants and independent celebrants are not the same thing: humanist celebrants conduct non-religious ceremonies only, while independent celebrants will include religious or spiritual content if you ask. In Scotland and Northern Ireland, also check your celebrant is legally authorised to marry you, since only authorised celebrants can.

Registrar fees differ by day of the week and by setting: a weekend ceremony at an approved venue costs several times a weekday register office slot. If the budget is tight, a weekday or an off-season date moves this line and usually the venue price too.
